text: Before CI exists, whether a change breaks anything depends entirely on one thing: whether the developer who made it remembered to run dbt build locally first. On a shared project, that's a recurring risk, not a survivable one.

Eventually someone merges a change that fails a real test on orders dot amount, and nobody notices until a business user sees a wrong number on a Power BI report. That's the concrete failure this chapter protects against.

A developer's clean local build only proves it worked against their own local state, at that moment. It doesn't prove the same build succeeds from a completely clean state, or give a reviewer any real confidence without re-running everything themselves.

Chapter 4 built real tests and dbt build as the mechanism that stops bad data from compounding — but on a laptop, that mechanism only runs if the developer runs it. CI is what turns a test that exists into a test that cannot be skipped.
On a shared project, no single person has the full picture of every model anymore. Running tests has to become structural, not a habit — which is exactly what the next two lessons build.
